ety.text: From Middle English faute, faulte, from Anglo-Norman faute, Old French faute, from Vulgar Latin *fallita (“shortcoming”), feminine of *fallitus, in place of Latin falsus, perfect passive participle of fallō (“deceive”). Displaced native Middle English schuld, schuild (“fault”) (from Old English scyld (“fault”)), Middle English lac (“fault, lack”) (from Middle Dutch lak (“lack, fault”)), Middle English last (“fault, vice”) (from Old Norse lǫstr (“fault, vice, crime”)). Compare French faute (“fault, foul”), Portuguese falta (“lack, shortage”) and Spanish falta (“lack, absence”).

senses.d: Culpability; the responsibility for a blameworthy event.
ex: No, don't blame yourself. It's my fault that we lost the game.
I told them the pie was still too hot. If they burn their tongues, that's their fault.

senses.d: A failing of character; less severe than a vice.
ex: Despite all her faults, she’s a good person at heart.

senses.d: A characteristic, positive or negative or both, which increases one's risk of danger or difficulty.
ex: You're still young, that's your fault.

senses.d: A strongly undesirable variation of food or drink caused by impurity or contamination.
ex: Cork taint is one of the most recognizable wine faults.

senses.d: A point of weakness in something's physical structure.
ex: As patches set upon a little breach / Discredit more in hiding of the fault.

senses.d: A minor offense.
An illegal serve.
A penalty point assessed in horseback events such as show jumping.
ex: If the horse refuses an obstacle, the rider will receive four faults.

senses.d: An exception within a software program or process.
A fracture in a rock formation causing a discontinuity.
To criticize, blame or find fault with something or someone.
ex: For that, says he, I ne'er will fault thee / But for humbleness exalt thee.

senses.d: To fracture.
To commit a mistake or error.
To undergo a page fault.
